name: Naltrexone/Bupropion (Contrave)
lead: Naltrexone/bupropion, sold as Contrave in the United States and Canada and as Mysimba in Europe, is a prescription tablet that combines an opioid-receptor blocker (naltrexone) with an antidepressant and smoking-cessation drug (bupropion). It is approved for chronic weight management in adults with obesity, or with overweight plus a weight-related condition, alongside a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity [2][4][12][27]. For people interested in appearance, its payoff is fat loss: by dampening appetite and food cravings it helps lower calorie intake, and the resulting weight reduction leaves the face, jawline, waist and overall physique leaner.

It was developed by Orexigen Therapeutics and approved by the US FDA on 10 September 2014 after an earlier rejection in February 2011, then authorised in the European Union in 2015 and in Canada in 2018 [27]. Phase 3 trials (COR-I, COR-II and COR-BMOD) compared the sustained-release combination with placebo over about 56 weeks and reported average weight losses of roughly 6 percent of body weight in the main trials and 9 percent when combined with intensive behavioural counselling [9][8][15][30]. Network meta-analyses place its average effect below that of semaglutide and tirzepatide [1][3][28].

Beyond obesity, the combination has been studied for binge-eating disorder, loss-of-control eating after bariatric surgery and methamphetamine use disorder [6][7][10][23][24]. Because both components are older, long-established medicines taken by mouth, Contrave is often discussed as a conventional, non-injectable option next to GLP-1 drugs [2][28].

paras: Clinical guidelines and reviews include naltrexone/bupropion among the approved medications for obesity, to be used together with lifestyle intervention [2][4][12][16]. The label indication covers adults with a body mass index of 30 or above, or 27 to under 30 with a weight-related condition such as type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia or controlled high blood pressure [27]. The 2022 American Gastroenterological Association guideline evaluated it alongside semaglutide, liraglutide, phentermine-topiramate, orlistat and other agents [16].
Researchers have also tested it for binge-eating disorder, loss-of-control eating after bariatric surgery and stimulant use disorders [7][11][23][24][6].

Weight loss is its appearance-relevant effect: as body fat falls, the face, jawline and waist become leaner and body composition shifts. In the trials, participants were also given diet and activity counselling, and the best results were seen in the group that received intensive behavioural support [15]. Average weight loss is smaller than with newer incretin drugs [1][3][28].

Bupropion inhibits reuptake of noradrenaline and dopamine, blocks nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and activates proopiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons in the hypothalamus, which lowers appetite and raises energy output [27][2]. Those neurons are restrained by a feedback loop driven by the body's own opioids, so adding naltrexone, a pure opioid antagonist, is intended to remove that brake and extend the appetite-suppressing signal [27][14].

The two drugs are described as acting on both hunger circuitry and the brain's reward pathway, reducing food cravings [27]. The concept drew on obesity neuroscience of the hypothalamic melanocortin system, including work by Monash University physiologist Michael Cowley, who received an Australian science honour in 2009 for work on these pathways [27].

Contrave is a trilayer, sustained-release tablet taken by mouth; the dose is stepped up over several weeks to a maintenance level [27]. A registered bioequivalence study compared tablets from two manufacturers in healthy volunteers [29].

COR-I, a multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial at 34 US sites, randomised 1,742 adults aged 18 to 65 to naltrexone plus bupropion at two dose levels or placebo for 56 weeks, with a mild reduced-calorie diet and exercise advice. Mean weight change was -1.3 percent with placebo, -5.0 percent at the lower dose and -6.1 percent at the higher dose; 16 percent of placebo participants lost at least 5 percent of body weight versus 39 and 48 percent. Only about half completed the 56 weeks. Nausea was the most frequent adverse event (about 27 to 30 percent versus 5 percent with placebo), and depression and suicidality were not increased [9][30].

COR-II randomised 1,496 adults 2:1 to the full combination or placebo for up to 56 weeks. Weight change at week 56 was -6.4 percent versus -1.2 percent, and 50.5 percent versus 17.1 percent lost at least 5 percent. Cardiometabolic markers, weight-related quality of life and control of eating also improved [8][30].

COR-BMOD added 28 group behaviour-modification sessions and an energy-reduced diet for both arms. In the modified intention-to-treat analysis, weight loss at week 56 was 9.3 percent with the combination and 5.1 percent with placebo plus behaviour modification; completers lost 11.5 and 7.3 percent [15][30].

A 2016 JAMA meta-analysis and later reviews place naltrexone/bupropion among the approved options that lower weight more than placebo [13][4]. A 2024 Lancet network meta-analysis of 132 trials (48,209 participants) reported that all weight-lowering drugs reduced bodyweight compared with lifestyle modification alone, with phentermine-topiramate the most effective among the older oral drugs [1]. A 2025 Nature Medicine network meta-analysis of 56 trials found all medications produced greater total body weight loss than placebo, with more than 10 percent for semaglutide and tirzepatide [3][28]. A 2024 JAMA review groups naltrexone/bupropion with centrally acting appetite drugs [2].

A 2022 American Journal of Psychiatry trial randomised 136 adults with binge-eating disorder and obesity to four 16-week arms. Binge-eating remission was 17.7 percent with placebo, 31.3 percent with naltrexone-bupropion, 37.1 percent with behavioural weight loss plus placebo and 57.1 percent with both; 5 percent weight loss rates were 11.8, 18.8, 31.4 and 38.2 percent [7][30]. Further trials examined maintenance treatment of binge-eating disorder [10][11].

In the NEJM ADAPT-2 trial, injectable naltrexone plus oral bupropion produced a weighted methamphetamine-response rate of 13.6 percent versus 2.5 percent with placebo in adults with moderate or severe methamphetamine use disorder [6][30]. A review of stimulant-withdrawal management also discusses the combination [5].

Registered phase 2 to 4 studies cover weight regain after bariatric surgery, weight maintenance after a behavioural programme, food addiction, breast cancer survivors and diabetes-remission diets [17][19][20][21][22][23][24].

A JAMA review reports constipation in about 20 percent of patients taking centrally acting weight-loss drugs, with nausea, headache and other effects varying by drug [2]. Nausea was the most common event in the phase 3 trials and was generally mild to moderate and transient [8][9]. Product information also lists insomnia, and reviews note effects on blood pressure and heart rate and a seizure risk tied to bupropion.

The FDA requires a boxed warning about suicidal thoughts and behaviour in children, adolescents and young adults under 25, attributed to bupropion as with all antidepressants. Safety and effectiveness in people under 18 have not been studied [27]. In COR-I and COR-II, depression and suicidality were not increased relative to placebo [9][8].

According to the FDA, the combination is contraindicated in people with a history of seizures or of an eating disorder such as bulimia or anorexia nervosa, in those taking opioids or in opioid withdrawal, within 14 days of a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, in pregnancy, and in people abruptly stopping alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates or antiepileptic drugs [27].

Orexigen Therapeutics submitted its New Drug Application in March 2010. In December 2010 an FDA advisory committee voted 13 to 7 to approve it and 11 to 8 to require a post-marketing cardiovascular outcomes study; on 2 February 2011 the FDA declined approval pending a large cardiovascular safety study [27].

The FDA approved the sustained-release formulation on 10 September 2014, and the European Medicines Agency's committee endorsed it that December, with EU authorisation in March 2015 [27]. In May 2015 a cardiovascular outcomes trial was stopped early after an independent panel said the company had inappropriately released interim data; a second trial, CONVENE, began in 2016 and was ended the same year after Takeda announced it would sell its US rights [27].

Takeda had marketed the product in the US under licence, with Orexigen receiving 20 percent of net sales as of 2015. In 2018 Orexigen sold its assets, including Contrave, to Nalpropion Pharmaceuticals, and Canada approved the drug the same year. The European committee completed a review of Mysimba in March 2025 [27].
Naltrexone/bupropion is prescription-only in the United States, Canada, the European Union and Australia (Schedule 4) [27]. It carries the ATC code A08AA62 among anti-obesity agents [27].

Naltrexone/bupropion is a brand-name medicine marketed by a pharmaceutical company and sits among the older oral options for weight management, discussed alongside phentermine-topiramate, orlistat and the newer injectable GLP-1 drugs [2][28]. In body-composition and fitness conversations it is mentioned as a prescription appetite suppressant that can be used while cutting, and as a pill-based alternative for people who prefer to avoid injections; its average results in published trials are lower than those of semaglutide and tirzepatide [1][3][28].
Registered phase 4 studies examine the metabolic and behavioural mechanisms of Contrave in obesity, its use in breast cancer survivors and its role in diabetes-remission programmes [18][19][22].

lore.intro: Naltrexone/bupropion is discussed in weight-loss and cutting conversations as the main oral, non-injectable prescription appetite option, usually in comparison with GLP-1 drugs [2][28].

claims.claim: Contrave is a pill alternative to GLP-1 injections
claims.believers: Advocates of oral options note it is taken by mouth, has been approved since 2014 and uses two long-established drugs [27][2].
claims.experts: Network meta-analyses report smaller average weight loss than semaglutide or tirzepatide, which exceeded 10 percent in the pooled trials [1][3][28].

claims.claim: It cuts cravings and 'food noise' by acting on reward pathways
claims.believers: Users and prescribers describe fewer cravings and less urge to snack, in line with the stated reward-pathway mechanism [27].
claims.experts: COR-II reported improved control of eating, and a binge-eating trial found higher remission with the drug than placebo (31.3 vs 17.7 percent) [8][7].

claims.claim: It helps get leaner for a sharper face and physique
claims.believers: People pursuing fat loss describe using appetite suppressants to sustain a calorie deficit while training.
claims.experts: Trials measured body weight, not facial or body composition, and weight loss occurred alongside diet and activity counselling [9][15].

claims.claim: It lifts mood and motivation through the bupropion component
claims.believers: Some patients describe more energy and drive, consistent with bupropion's dopamine and noradrenaline action [27].
claims.experts: Phase 3 trials found no increase in depression or suicidality, while the label carries a boxed warning for people under 25 [8][9][27].

claims.claim: It can curb stimulant and compulsive-eating urges
claims.believers: Researchers and patients point to the reward-circuit action as relevant beyond weight loss [27].
claims.experts: The NEJM methamphetamine trial reported low but higher response (13.6 vs 2.5 percent), and registered trials examine post-bariatric loss-of-control eating [6][23][24].

claims.claim: It prevents weight regain after bariatric surgery
claims.believers: Patients with regain describe it as an option to restart loss.
claims.experts: Small registered phase 2 to 4 studies are listed, and results are not reported in the registry entries [21][23][24].

card.summary: Prescription pill pairing an opioid blocker with an antidepressant for appetite control; solid but modest weight loss next to GLP-1 drugs.
card.note: Prescription-only; bupropion carries warnings on mood and seizures.

quick.overview:
Contrave is a daily extended-release tablet combining naltrexone and bupropion. It is approved to help adults with obesity or overweight lose weight alongside diet and exercise.
Trials report weight loss over placebo, but network meta-analyses place it below semaglutide and tirzepatide.
quick.mechanism: Bupropion raises dopamine and noradrenaline and activates appetite-suppressing neurons in the hypothalamus, while naltrexone blocks the opioid feedback that would otherwise damp that effect, so the pair reduce appetite and cravings.
quick.risks: Reviews note constipation in about 20% of users of centrally acting weight drugs; nausea, headache and insomnia are also reported. Bupropion carries warnings about suicidal thoughts and seizure risk and can raise blood pressure. Prescription-only.

angle.text: Contrave is a prescription medicine used to reduce body weight, which changes how the face and body look as fat is lost. In trials its average effect is smaller than that of semaglutide or tirzepatide, and it is prescribed alongside diet and activity changes.
